analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new oil and gas drilling leases off the California coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Natural Resources subcommittee after being introduced in April 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently prohibit oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities in federal waters off California's coast. It would not affect drilling rights under leases already issued. It was introduced by four California Democrats and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: California coastal communities, including tourism businesses, commercial and recreational fishing, and residents whose beaches, fisheries, and coastal economies are exposed to oil spill risk from new offshore drilling. Offshore spill risk from new platforms falls on coastal towns whose livelihoods depend on clean water and beaches.
analysis.who_benefits_short: California coastal communities and fishing economies

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities in outer Continental Shelf areas off the California coast, foreclosing any future federal sale of new drilling leases there [S2] [S3].

The ban is written to last: it is added directly to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and overrides other provisions of that law and any other law, so a future administration could not simply add California waters to a leasing plan [S3].
It preserves rights under leases already issued before enactment, so existing operators keep their contractual interests and only new drilling is barred [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that might otherwise bid on new federal offshore leases off California, and the federal Treasury to the extent those leases would have produced bonus bids and royalties. No one currently operating under an existing lease loses anything.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking new leases

drawbacks.text: It would permanently remove a potential source of federal royalty revenue and domestic energy production; offshore drilling bans trade possible revenue and energy supply for avoided spill risk, and critics argue elected bodies should weigh that trade rather than lock it in by statute [S2] [S3].

The bill protects California waters only, leaving the question of where new offshore drilling should and should not occur to a state-by-state patchwork rather than a comprehensive national policy [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is risk reduction for coastal communities and ecosystems that bear the damage if a spill occurs, while the cost is forgone drilling revenue and production concentrated in one region. The existing-lease carve-out limits disruption to current operators, which makes the design narrow and targeted. The main weakness is not design but the fact that it never received any committee or floor consideration, so no trade-off was ever publicly debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps introduced the California Ocean and Coastal Protection Act on April 22, 2015, with Reps. Farr, Lowenthal, and Huffman joining as original cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the day it was introduced [S5].
On May 19, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action is recorded for the remainder of the 114th Congress [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House, and no Senate companion action is recorded [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: oil and gas companies retain the possibility that future administrations could include California offshore waters in a federal leasing plan, since no statutory ban was enacted. California coastal communities gained no new legal protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas firms seeking future leases

for.name: Rep. Lois Capps
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to permanently bar new oil and gas leasing off California's coast.

for.name: Reps. Sam Farr, Alan Lowenthal, and Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore energy leasing
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee without scheduling a hearing or markup; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were California Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no record exists of how the full House or any committee would have split.

industries.note: The bill would bar the industry from new preleasing and leasing in federal waters off California, while leaving existing leases untouched. Offshore expansion profits the industry but places spill risk on coastal communities, so its interest here runs against the bill's beneficiaries.
A permanent ban on new offshore drilling reduces the chance of a spill damaging beaches, fisheries, and the tourism economy those businesses depend on.
